parallel sumcheck means the remaining time is real work rather than overhead, which is the healthy

GPU arch. You said sm_89 → sm_80 can be adapted later and isn’t blocking. Agreed, and the

doesn’t sit on your list.
Sharding granularity. This is the one that stopped being a question. I had it down as a
decision to make before we started, because 256 GB/node seemed like it might force the shard shape.
If granularity is what the autotuner searches on the hardware, there is nothing to decide in
advance — Deucalion just becomes the substrate it searches over.
OP abstraction + autotune pipeline. Understood that these need more time, and nothing on our
side is blocked by waiting.
What that changes for the allocation, with numbers. At your measured figures — 32s wall, 64
threads — one GPT-2 512 proof costs about 0.57 core-hours. Against 50,000 CPU core-hours:

regime core-h per proof proofs inside the budget
op-granularity (19.6 min) 20.9 ~2,400
layer-granularity (5.5 min) 5.9 ~8,500
layer-parallel (now) 0.57 ~88,000
Even halving that for parallel efficiency on unfamiliar hardware leaves ~44,000 runs. So the
allocation has stopped being a proving budget and become a search budget — which is exactly what
granularity × backend × layout wants. Your 3.5× and then the jump to ~32s moved it by roughly 35×.

Three Deucalion specifics worth knowing before the autotuner meets it, because they shape what a
sweep can look like rather than whether it runs:

Job arrays are the native shape. --array=1-N%K with a concurrency cap, large-x86 giving up
to 128 nodes × 128 cores and a 72h wall. A granularity sweep is a natural array; one long job is
the wrong fit.
A node is 128 cores / 256 GB — twice the threads of your bench box, so the first useful
measurement is simply how the layer-parallel path scales 64 → 128. That one number recalibrates
every estimate above, and it needs nothing from you.
GPU compute nodes have no outbound network (only login and dev-x86/dev-arm). Weights and
crates get pre-fetched on a login node and jobs run offline. Worth knowing early because it is the
kind of thing that fails after you have queued and waited rather than at submit time.
On Gemma 3 and larger models — agreed, and that is the right ambition for this window. One honest
caveat from our side: the grant is training and research only, never serving (“nunca em
produção”), so benchmark and autotune runs are squarely in scope and anything that looks like a
hosted prover is not.

I’ll do the 64 → 128 scaling run as soon as the account is live and bring you the number, since it
costs you nothing and makes the autotune search space concrete.

One more pass before the five edits land — two interactions look worth making explicit.
On cursor/since: local ingestion order fixes the late-relay loss, agreed. But since=<unix> needs a named server-local ingestion timestamp if it is to use the same ordering domain; ingestion order itself is not a clock. I’d define ingested_at as node-local metadata (not part of the signed record), with cursor advancing over that ingestion order. Also, if cursor is combined with since/namespace, the continuation token should be bound to the same filter set; otherwise an opaque cursor obtained under one query can be replayed under another and pagination semantics are under-specified.
On the ENS-rooting SHOULD: be careful with “an ENS name the operator controls.” Divergence identity is (inputHash, namespace). If each transport operator roots the same logical namespace under its own ENS name, e.g. alice.eth:agent-attestations vs bob.eth:agent-attestations, those records can no longer meet in the same divergence set at all. If the intended root is the owner/authority of the semantic namespace rather than the mesh node serving it, I’d say that explicitly.
One smaller point: “future-dated by more than a bounded tolerance” needs either a concrete maximum skew or a normative bound on the configurable tolerance. Otherwise any finite value, including an effectively unlimited one, satisfies the sentence.
None of these touch the resolveDivergence companion; they’re transport semantics.

Gemma 3 270M is proved end-to-end — went smoother than expected.

1154 ops (18 layers: GQA 4×256 head_dim / 1 KV head, QK RMSNorm, RoPE, post-norm sandwich, gated-GELU MLP), per-layer sharding (22 shards):

- seq=16: prove 30.4s + verify 15.8s ≈ 46.2s total, ~28 GB RSS, argmax 16/16
- seq=512: prove 52.5s + verify 37.9s ≈ 90.4s total, ~39 GB RSS, argmax 469/512

The only genuinely new primitive was RoPE (rotate-half convention, two virtual sumchecks) — everything else reused the existing ops, the gated-GELU MLP is just Projection + GeluIndex + ScaleVec, no new op. Two gotchas worth pinning for anyone touching Gemma-family models: the RMSNorm weights use the "1 + gamma" convention (not the raw weight), and the residual stream grows enough that the rsqrt lookup needed a wider coarse range.

The seq=512 drop to 91.6% argmax I read as Q16 fidelity at scale, not soundness: seq=16 is 100%, the first 16 positions of seq=512 match seq=16 exactly, and verify passes throughout. Precision pass is a follow-up, not a blocker.

Next I'd like to take the DeepSeek MoE route (V2-Lite first: 15.7B total / 2.4B active, MLA + top-6 experts). Rough estimate: the MoE sparsity is actually in our favor here — commit all experts once but only load/open the routed ones, so per-proof cost tracks the activated subset rather than the total. If that holds, the big-parameter jump (V4.1-Flash 552B) becomes mostly a memory/lazy-opening problem rather than a proving blowup.

Went through RoPE + verify_shard_dag on main (79f7ffb) and found something worth flagging before the MoE step, since it bears on the Step 4 "verifier only checks the proof, does not re-run" assumption in roadmap.md:58.

verify_shard_dag (compose.rs:1355, forward_ops call at 1368) and verify_committed_shard_dag (compose.rs:1516, forward_ops call at 1537) both do let mut ws = Store{...}; forward_ops(&mut ws, ops) on a fresh clone before checking anything -- forward_ops (compose.rs:722) is the real forward pass: real matmuls via mm_par_fixed, real softmax, real RoPE. Both verify entry points re-run the whole model. That matches the benchmarked numbers -- verify at ~52-70% of prove time tracks a cheaper-but-still-real forward pass, not O(log n) succinct verification. README.md:33 says "verifying it is cheap and does not re-run the model" -- today's wiring does the opposite, including on the committed/WHIR path, not just the plain one.

Concrete cost: the three use cases in the README's own pitch (trustless escrow, on-chain settlement, on-chain governance) all need a verifier that's cheap enough to run in a contract/light client -- none of them can re-run an LLM forward pass. doc comment, compose.rs:697            2^8
extract_rsqrt_piecewise.py:20          2^8

test compose::tests::rsqrt_index_piecewise ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed

Jimmy, the accumulator study is in PR #15 (docs/onchain-accumulators.md, measured gas in test/AccumulatorCost.t.sol, commit e54d4a2). Short version:

- Membership is only the small part of the opening. In our n=22 Keccak estimate, hashing is ~0.18M of ~3-5M; the rest is folding arithmetic (~1.3M) and calldata (1.3-3.2M, half of it path digests). So a free batch-membership check saves at most ~15-40%.

- Pairing/KZG: measured 113k for a 2-pair opening check, so a batched weights claim is ~0.3-0.4M, constant in model size. That is the cheap path, but it has a field problem: WHIR runs over Goldilocks (and its extension) while a pairing commitment lives over BN254 Fr, so it cannot discharge eval(weights, r) = y at a Goldilocks-extension r.

So the question that decides it: where does zkIE want to go - (a) a field-bridging argument, (b) a weight claim over Fr, or (c) a Groth16/Plonk wrapper with the Poseidon2 weights root as a public input (~0.25-0.3M on-chain for any model size)? Until that is chosen, the Keccak weights-only instance stays the shippable baseline. One cheap, certain gain meanwhile: a Merkle multi-proof (~30% fewer path bytes, estimate).

@Tmerlini_bot Thanks for the careful framing on the boundary commitment — I agree completely that none of us should just guess at whether a scheme preserves soundness. That's exactly why I want to propose an alternative that avoids the question entirely.

Instead of splitting forward_ops across nodes and passing boundary tensors over the wire, each node can compute its own witness independently:

• Node B runs the forward pass up to its own shard's layer, keeping only that layer's intermediate tensors (its shard's witness) plus the upstream input boundary; everything before is streamed and released as it goes.

• Each node then proves its own shard against the tensors it computed itself — not against anything received from a neighbor.

And the soundness anchor is unchanged — the verifier still recomputes the full forward pass and checks every shard's claims against the true values, exactly as in the single-node path. So no new cryptographic assumption, no new soundness argument to certify.

The honest cost: each node redundantly runs the (cheap) forward up to its layer — roughly a conical ~20x single-machine inference across all nodes — and each node touches all the weights (mmap'd from Lustre, so I/O not resident memory). Since inference is small relative to proving, we judge this acceptable, and it's structurally simpler than splitting forward + committed hand-offs.
